entry.title: Dowsers – “Dogwood” & “Three Forks Of Cheat”
entry.summary: The new North Carolina/Illinois sextet Dowsers brings together members of some of the best bands in the experimental folk-rock underground. The personnel: Courtney Werner and Evan Morgan (Magic Tuber Stringband, Weirs), Austin Cash (solo artist, Nathan Smearage), Oliver Child-Lanning (Weirs, Sluice, Fust), James Gibian (Beak Trio), and Alli Rogers (Alli Blois). As a person who…
entry.content:
The new North Carolina/Illinois sextet Dowsers brings together members of some of the best bands in the experimental folk-rock underground. The personnel: Courtney Werner and Evan Morgan (Magic Tuber Stringband, Weirs), Austin Cash (solo artist, Nathan Smearage), Oliver Child-Lanning (Weirs, Sluice, Fust), James Gibian (Beak Trio), and Alli Rogers (Alli Blois). As a person who has blogged many an excited blog post about acts from that world, I was delighted to learn about this crew.

Hearing their music was delightful too. Dowsers, who also organize a music festival called FEAST, are announcing their signing to Gar Hole Records today with a pair of new tracks: "Dogwood," a slow-swaying roots-rock ballad, and "Three Forks Of Cheat," a rustic post-rock instrumental based on an old Edden Hammons fiddle tune. Both songs are well worth hearing, and you may enjoy this context from Morgan:

“Dogwood” is a song that I wrote in the spring of 2020 at my friend Hunter's grandparents' house in Hayesville, NC so it's release has been a long-time coming. The reliability of certain seasonal markers, some familiar and some new depending on local ecosystems shifting conditions due to climate change, is something I think we all become increasingly aware of as we grow older. The Dogwood tree that grew outside this house in Hayesville was the center here for my reflection on humans growing older but natural cycles reappearing.

“Three Forks of Cheat” has always been one of my favorite fiddle tunes. The source fiddler for this one is Edden Hammons of Webster County, WV. I learned it from playing with Will Csorba who shared his obsession with me for Hammons family tunes. I think of the three unequal, "crooked" lines of the B part as representing the three forks of the Cheat River. I wanted to try to draw out the atmospheric qualities of this strange tune with Dowsers, ending in a cacophonous sludge section inspired by the great Athens band Harvey Milk.

Listen below.

entry.content:
Kid Cudi is the ultimate multi-hyphenate. The rapper has done memoirs, funnel cake mix, and Star Trek brand ambassadorships. He's also done a lot of acting, including in the slasher hit X and the animated Netflix series Entergalactic. Now, he's announcing a Basquiat biopic.

"JEAN. Written, directed and starring me. Filming 2027," his post on Instagram begins. It continues:

For years people have asked me about playing Jean Michel Basquiat in a film. But no project actually came to be. This year, I finally said fuck it, ima write it myself. Did a wardrobe test, got a wig made (this isnt the final just a rough, trust me we gon get it perfect). But I wanted to tease what we been cooking a bit. This one im so proud of and excited about. To write a film about someone who existed was a challenge, but it was a welcomed one. A lot of research, books, talks with people that knew him. This film will be a love letter to Jean, the 80s and NY city. Jean has inspired me all through out my career, and it will be the biggest honor to tell his story in a way we haven't seen before. I know a lot of yall gon be like FINALLY hahaha I love it. This ones for all those dreamers out there.

entry.content:
Since 2022, Marley Guevara has been releasing swoony indie pop under the moniker Maz. She even transformed Dinosaur Jr.'s "Little Fury Things" into a synth-pop wonderland. Now, the Utah artist is announcing her new EP Loveandpain and sharing the title track.

"'Loveandpain' was written with my great-grandfather's ghost, drawing from his helpless romantic spirit," Guevara says. "The song, to me, explores love and pain as two sides of the same coin, the deepest pain you've felt existing alongside the deepest joy and ultimately choosing to love fully, even when you know that love can hurt."

While working on the EP, Guevara came across long-forgotten tapes of her great-grandfather singing and playing guitar. Not only did she use them as inspiration, but she also sampled them. Hear the title track below.

entry.content:
Ben Folds Five are reuniting for their first tour in 14 years. The sardonic piano-rockers got together for a one-off hometown show at the storied North Carolina venue Cat's Cradle in 2023, but they haven't hit the road together since their last reunion tour wrapped up in 2013. The occasion for the outing would appear to be BFF's recent deluxe reissue of their 1995 debut album, though maybe Folds has more time on his hands since leaving the Kennedy Center last year.

In April, Folds, bassist Robert Sledge, and drummer Darren Jessee will reconvene for nine shows across the American South. It's the first leg of what we're told will be a more extensive tour, so Foldsheads across the nation need not worry. Tickets go on sale this Friday, Oct. 23 at 10 a.m. local time. entry.content:
Fenne Lily's new album Win Win arrives at the end of the week. The British singer-songwriter has shared "Uh Huh," "Thank You Sorry," and "Sleeping," and today she's back with one final preview called "Stranger Things."

"I thought the title would expand my listenership to include people looking for the Stranger Things soundtrack," the artist quips. "The title actually came before the song, inspired by something else my dad said when I was going through it. He reminded me that everything you find and miss is proof that there are more brilliant things out there. That you're lucky to find one, and you will again."

"Stranger Things" is a twangy daydream that comes with an idyllic music video shot in Seattle's Puget Sound by Jolie M-A. Watch below.

Win Win is out 10/23 on Nettwerk.

entry.content:
Earlier this month, Doechii revived Swamp Sessions, the extremely cool video series that she launched before the release of her star-making 2024 mixtape Alligator Bites Never Heal. The Swamp Session videos were all short, cinematic, eye-grabbing clips for the energetic songs that later appeared on that tape. These days, Doechii is working on what's being billed as her debut album, and we already posted a Swamp Session clip for a new song called "Bomb." Last night, she dropped another one.

Doechii co-directed her new two-minute "Catwoman" video with Carlos Acosta, and we don't know whether it's the full song or an excerpt or what. (It's not on streaming yet.) The clip opens with Doechii posing in a desert mountain landscape, rapping hard and emphatically over a tingly boom-bap beat. Then, something dramatic happens. I'd rather not spoil it. See it for yourself below.

I've seen pop stars do this gimmick when introducing their new personas before, but I don't think I've ever seen it rendered quite so vividly.

entry.content:
It's official: A new Chvrches album is on the way. The Scottish synthpop trio released Screen Violence, their most recent LP, in 2021. Since then, lead singer Lauren Mayberry has gone solo, and so has Martin Doherty with his new project the Leaving. Last month, Chvrches came back with the new single "Roses." That was our first taste of All The King's Men, the new album set to come out early next year.

After working remotely on Screen Violence, all three Chvrches reconvened in Glasgow, the city that only one Chvrch currently inhabits, to make All The King’s Men. In addition to "Roses," the LP includes "Conman," a new song that the band debuted live earlier this year. They don't have a new song today, but they have unveiled plans for an international tour that'll kick off in February. Below, check out the album's tracklist and those dates.

entry.content:
Chip City, bitch. Chip Chip City, bitch. What do you think life is like in Chip City? I bet it's pretty good. I bet there's lots of chips. When you're watching TV and you've already eaten dinner but you're still just a tiny bit hungry, I bet that's the place to be. Just speculating, though. To confirm, you'd have to check with My Wonderful Boyfriend. That's the name of the band. I don't have a wonderful boyfriend. My boyfriend ain't shit.

The Brooklyn indie trio My Wonderful Boyfriend landed on our list of 2024's best new bands before they'd even released their debut EP An Evening With... The band followed that record with the one-off single "I'm Your Man" last year, and now they're celebrating their new deal with New West Records by releasing "Chip City," a scraggly, creaky new jam rooted in the early Modest Mouse style that never quite goes away.

In a press release, My Wonderful Boyfriend frontman PJ McCormick says, "This is a love song from a guy who is a little drunker than he thinks he is. He's a romantic, but he isn't really finding the right words. He's putting all his eggs in one basket, and it isn't wise. He's losing the plot. There's maybe a line or two in the outro where he sobers up enough to get the picture." Check out the Godfrey Nares-directed video below.

entry.title: If It Rains Release Crushing New EP All We’ve Got
entry.summary: Evan Stein used to be a member of Anklebiter and Broken Vow, two extremely sick young straight edge hardcore bands from the Northeast. These days, Stein leads If It Rains, another band that fits right into the lineage. If It Rains’ style is all passionately ferocious chug that recalls bands like Turning Point and Have…
entry.content:
Evan Stein used to be a member of Anklebiter and Broken Vow, two extremely sick young straight edge hardcore bands from the Northeast. These days, Stein leads If It Rains, another band that fits right into the lineage. If It Rains' style is all passionately ferocious chug that recalls bands like Turning Point and Have Heart at their most dramatic. And hey, look at that, they're about to play one of Have Heart's upcoming reunion shows, and they've got Have Heart frontman Pat Flynn on their new EP.

If It Rains released their hugely promising demo in 2024 and followed it with a two-song single last year. Yesterday, they made good on all that promise with a heavy, powerful, and surprisingly exploratory EP called All We've Got. It's got all the big heart-on-sleeve mosh moments that I want from music like this, but it also stretches out on tracks like the impressive six-minute epic "In Another Life." The EP ends with "But This Life Is All We've Got," a song that features Have Heart/Fiddlehead leader Pat Flynn and Sign Language's Sarah Tolley. Really cool record. Check it out below.

The All We've Got EP is out now on Delayed Gratification.

Angine de Poitrine are the band of the moment, or at least a band of the moment. The costumed microtonal math-rockers have a zany, eye-catching look and a sound to match, and their glow-up this past year — including a Polaris Prize win, the emergence of tribute bands, and encounters with the likes of Shania Twain — suggests they've been giving a lot of people something they didn't know they wanted. If you've been playing and replaying their KEXP session and Fallon performance, now's your chance to witness their show in real life, just like our own Tom Breihan did last month.

The band already had a fairly robust, fully sold-out tour scheduled through the end of this year, but now they've added dates all over the world for 2027. From March through July, they'll be hitting Oceania, North and South America, and Europe. Hopefully they've figured out a good laundry situation for those outfits because they're going to get a lot of wear.

entry.summary: In a few weeks, my former boss, the Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber, will publish his memoir Weird Era: How Pitchfork Changed Music Forever. I’ve already read the book, and a lot of it is Schreiber giving his hindsight-enhanced reflections on the big moments in Pitchfork’s history. So you better believe he’s got some things to…
entry.content:
In a few weeks, my former boss, the Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber, will publish his memoir Weird Era: How Pitchfork Changed Music Forever. I've already read the book, and a lot of it is Schreiber giving his hindsight-enhanced reflections on the big moments in Pitchfork's history. So you better believe he's got some things to say about Clap Your Hands Say Yeah, the previously unheralded indie band who got a big boost when Pitchfork raved about their self-titled 2005 debut and who then became a symbol of, and perhaps a punchline about, the site's starmaking powers. Anyway, Clap Your Hands Say Yeah endure, and they've got a new album on the way.

Alec Ounsworth, the only core member of Clap Your Hands Say Yeah, spent last year marking the 20th anniversary of the band's debut with a tour and a reissue. Early in 2027, they'll release Burned, the first CYHSY album in more than six years. Lead single "Fever Of The Mind" is a big, sweeping, passionate piece of old-school indie rock that feels very, very comforting for those of us who were there. It's a nice little reminder of why Pitchfork liked those guys in the first place. Below, check out that song and the dates for the band's 2027 tour.

entry.title: Cloud Nothings Announce New Album What Kind of Hell Did You Survive?: Hear “Death Keeps Me Alive”
entry.summary: For more something like a decade and a half, if not longer, Cloud Nothings have been among the most consistent forces on the indie rock landscape. But maybe they’re itching to get out of that landscape and explore some different ones. These days, Cloud Nothings record for Pure Noise, a label mostly rooted in post-hardcore.…
entry.content:
For more something like a decade and a half, if not longer, Cloud Nothings have been among the most consistent forces on the indie rock landscape. But maybe they're itching to get out of that landscape and explore some different ones. These days, Cloud Nothings record for Pure Noise, a label mostly rooted in post-hardcore. Two years ago, they dropped a Misfits cover on a Pure Noise comp. And today, Cloud Nothings announce plans to follow 2024's Final Summer with What Kind of Hell Did You Survive?, a new album that's sonically rooted in metal and heavy rock.

If you ever heard their 2012 classic Attack On Memory, then you already know Cloud Nothings can get truly heavy when they want. Drummer Jayson Gerycz is a mega-beast who can play fast and heavy at the same time. So the idea of a metal-influenced Cloud Nothings album isn't that much of a stretch. Still, it's fun to hear them shift into that gear without losing their personality on new single "Death Keeps Me Alive." (Sick title.) It's a vaguely doomy riff-monster that made me think of both Cave-In and the Wipers, and it even gets a tiny bit black metal toward the end.

Here's what frontman Dylan Baldi says about the new album and about "Death Keeps Me Alive" in particular:

The album is our attempt to pay homage to the heavy rock music we've been listening to over the last few years. Some pretty direct and popular musical influences on the tracks are Queens of the Stone Age, Motörhead, Earth, and Electric Wizard. We were feeling a little pigeonholed in the indie rock world and wanted to make a change in our sound that revealed a different facet of our interests and abilities...

Lyrically, I was inspired by a lot of more political metal and hardcor. The songs deal with cruel governments, the importance of community, and occasionally a general rage at the state of the world...

Lyrically, "Death Keeps Me Alive" is from the point of view of a lurking evil power that never gets fully defeated in the world and feeds off of death, war, and hate, which is kind of a fun generically "metal" thing to sing about. I hope people hear this song and get excited for what the rest of the record could possibly sound like, and recognize that this is going to be a new version of Cloud Nothings that didn't really have a precedent prior to this recording.

Alex Scalzo-Brown directed the black-and-white "Death Keeps Me Alive" video, which has some fun spooky-season vibes. Below, check out that clip, the What Kind of Hell Did You Survive? tracklist, and Cloud Nothings' upcoming tour dates.

entry.content:
In just a few days, the indie rock singer-songwriter Caroline Rose will release Gentling The Horse At The Walt Whitman Mall, the new album that they recorded with producer John Congleton. We've posted their singles "Chow Mein," "Calm," and "Hello Again, Jim." With the album release looming, Rose has just shared one more track, "Valery (please don't be mad at me) It's a bright, propulsive power-pop number that builds to some awesomely erratic screamy stuff. Here's what Rose says about the song:

A lot of this record pulls from stories from my hometown and fuses them with other stories from when I lived in NYC, so some characters might be a mix of two or three different people. "Valery" is a combination of my best friend from my hometown, who passed away from a heroin overdose many years ago, along with another friend I loved so much who also became addicted to heroin and just had a really difficult life. I gravitate toward people in my life who have struggled, and they often come out as characters in my songs.

Below, check out the studio version of "Valery (please don't be mad at me)," as well as a video of Rose and their band playing the song live at Permanent Records in LA.

Gentling The Horse At The Walt Whitman Mall is out 10/23 on Rose's own label SUCK records.

Back in 2023 and 2024, we posted his singles “Dream All Night,” “Century,” and “Baby.” Eiger took some time off from releasing new music, but…
entry.content:
Isaac Eiger used to be the frontman of the New York indie pop band Strange Ranger. Right after their breakup, he started making his own music under the name Threshold. Back in 2023 and 2024, we posted his singles "Dream All Night," "Century," and "Baby." Eiger took some time off from releasing new music, but he came back yesterday with the new song "Stillwater."

It's not that Isaac Eiger hasn't been busy. In the time since his 2024 mini-album Thief, he has racked up songwriting credits on records from ADÉLA, Chanel Beads, and Frost Children, and he plays bass in the New York band Voyeur. Threshold, meanwhile, is his vehicle for old-school stripped-down singer-songwriter music, and that's what "Stillwater" is. It's a graceful midtempo piano ballad with a heartstring-tugging chorus, and I don't know whether it has anything to do with the band from Almost Famous. Below, check out the Daniel Patrick Brennan-directed "Stillwater" video and Threshold's upcoming live shows.

entry.title: Wendy Eisenberg Releases Surprise New Companion Album Wweennddyy Eeiisseennbbeerrgg
entry.summary: Factoring in Wendy Eisenberg’s solo material and various collaborations, their collected output is all over the map: from skronking rock to intimate folk, from pop structure to experimental abstraction. On their acclaimed self-titled album this year, Eisenberg leaned into their singer-songwriter side. But there’s more than one way to approach those songs. Today Eisenberg has…
entry.content:
Factoring in Wendy Eisenberg's solo material and various collaborations, their collected output is all over the map: from skronking rock to intimate folk, from pop structure to experimental abstraction. On their acclaimed self-titled album this year, Eisenberg leaned into their singer-songwriter side. But there's more than one way to approach those songs.

Today Eisenberg has surprise-released Wweennddyy Eeiisseennbbeerrgg, a new companion album comprising extended versions of two Wendy Eisenberg tracks. Recording with bassist Trevor Dunn, violinist Mari Rubio (more eaze), and drummer Ryan Sawyer, Eisenberg created a stunning 37-minute version of lead single "Meaning Business" and a nine-minute edition of closer "The Walls." Naturally, they're now titled "Mmeeaanniinngg Bbuussiinneess" and "Tthhee Wwaallllss." The resulting 46-minute collection is longer than the original LP, and it serves as a reminder of how adventurous and versatile this artist can be.

A statement from Eisenberg:

I want to write songs that feel infinite. I want to write songs that transcend their production, that can weather the changes. It’s probably a holdover from my jazz training, the desire to hear my material in different contexts. A standard sounds different passed through time and hands. This band, Ryan Mari and Trevor, can do anything- between them their practices span jazz, metal, country, ambient music, minimalism, and hyperpop, at least. Why not literally stretch them, and my songs, out? I want to feel when a slowed-down song becomes ambient music, becomes jazz, becomes something else. Experimental music; an experiment. Hopefully not chopped, but definitely a little screwed.

Subjecting these two songs, songs that are explicitly about memory, to a compositional process explicitly about length, lets me perceive the time in each song differently. In these versions, the form is maintained but sections elide, become solos, become worlds. Returning to the chorus feels different after fifteen minutes than it does after a minute and a half. Maybe it’s a Cagean imposition, making a pop song stay interesting after 20 minutes. I can justify it however, forever. I just want to hear the band play on.

Stream Wweennddyy Eeiisseennbbeerrgg below.

entry.title: Beck Plays The Tonight Show With Sacha Baron Cohen On Cello
entry.summary: Every once in a while, Beck dips back into an old, reliable well and makes an album of bummed-out, heavily orchestrated acoustic music. That’s the mode that he was in on Mutations, Sea Change, and Morning Phase — great records all. Last month, he released Ride Lonesome, his latest in that unofficial series. On Tuesday…
entry.content:
Every once in a while, Beck dips back into an old, reliable well and makes an album of bummed-out, heavily orchestrated acoustic music. That's the mode that he was in on Mutations, Sea Change, and Morning Phase — great records all. Last month, he released Ride Lonesome, his latest in that unofficial series. On Tuesday night, Beck was a guest on Jimmy Fallon's Tonight Show. He performed "In The Night," his new LP's lead single, with a full string section behind him, including fellow Tonight Show guest Sacha Baron Cohen on cello.

Did you know Sacha Baron Cohen played cello? Well, he does. In 2020, Cohen told The New York Times that his first TV appearance was playing cello on something called Fanfare For Young Musicians. Cohen was on Fallon to promote his new movie Ali G: Who Iz I?, and I would love to know who asked for that. He did not play cello in character as Ali G, which might've been interesting. Instead, we just got the slightly distracting image of this one famous guy studiously and unfunnily sawing at his instrument during what was generally a lovely performance. Watch it below.

On last night's episode, Beck also sat for an interview with Jimmy Fallon. The two of them did a little 5-10-15-20 bit, with Beck talking about some of the records that influenced him: the Snow White And The Seven Dwarfs soundtrack, Mississippi John Hurt, Gary Wilson, Kraftwerk. He and Questlove also reminisced about playing some shows together back in the '90s, and he mentioned that Hansel, the Owen Wilson character in Zoolander, was at least partially based on him, which I can kind of see. Beck claimed that he turned down a cameo in Zoolander and that the part went to David Bowie instead. Bowie crushed that performance, so we're probably better off with the way things happened. Here's the interview.

Ride Lonesome is out now on Capitol. Sacha Baron Cohen's Ali G movie comes out on Friday, and so does its soundtrack album. That record is executive produced by Andrew Watt and Hit-Boy, and Jon Batiste is on it. The single "Richer Than Elon," this month's second soundtrack song about Elon Musk, is out now.

entry.title: Spotify Rolls Out AI Persona Badges, Removes 75 Million “Spammy Tracks”
entry.summary: Over the summer, Spotify finally announced a plan to deal with the onslaught of AI slop, which involved “AI Persona” badges for AI-generated artists and keeping their music out of recommended playlists. In a new statement, the streaming service says they’ve removed over 75 million “spammy tracks” from the platform. The statement also says they’ve…
entry.content:
Over the summer, Spotify finally announced a plan to deal with the onslaught of AI slop, which involved "AI Persona" badges for AI-generated artists and keeping their music out of recommended playlists. In a new statement, the streaming service says they've removed over 75 million "spammy tracks" from the platform.

The statement also says they've pulled more than 50 million slop and spam tracks out of recommendations and labeled thousands of artist profiles with AI Persona badges. In addition, artists who release AI-assisted songs have the option to identify AI in the song credits.

"No single signal catches slop or spam on its own, so we combine many: listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and information from multiple third-party AI detection tools," the statement reads. "AI detection technology in particular has limitations, and it will only get harder as generative AI evolves. Using these signals together, we can identify likely slop or spam with more confidence. We also hunt for new tactics, including mass uploads, duplicates, SEO manipulation, spammy playlist networks, and artificially short tracks. As spammers change tactics, we'll keep updating our systems."

Read the full statement here.
